blocks.content: DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (DPSP)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are contained in Part IV (Articles 36–51) and aim to establish a welfare state.
The concept of DPSP is borrowed from the Irish Constitution and represents moral and political obligations of the State.
DPSPs are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be directly enforced by courts of law.
They are categorized into Socialistic Principles, Gandhian Principles, and Liberal–Intellectual Principles.
The Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills Case (1980) ruled that the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
INTRODUCTION

blocks.content: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are an important part of the Indian Constitution. They are mentioned in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36 to 51).

The Directive Principles act as guidelines to the State for establishing a just and welfare society. Although they are not enforceable by courts, they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
CONCEPT AND MEANING OF DPSP
The Directive Principles of State Policy are directions given to the State to follow while framing laws and policies.
They aim to:

items:
• Establish a welfare state
  • Promote social and economic justice
  • Reduce inequalities
  • Improve living standards of people
Establish a welfare state
Promote social and economic justice
Reduce inequalities
Improve living standards of people

blocks.content: The concept of DPSP is borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
NATURE OF DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES

items:
• DPSPs are non-justiciable in nature
  • Courts cannot enforce them
  • However, the State should apply them while making laws
  • They are moral and political obligations of the State

blocks.content: Though non-enforceable, DPSPs are considered fundamental to governance.
CLASSIFICATION OF DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES
Directive Principles are generally classified into three categories:

items: Socialistic Principles
Gandhian Principles
Liberal–Intellectual Principles

blocks.content: The Directive Principles of State Policy form the soul of the Indian Constitution.
SOCIALISTIC PRINCIPLES
These principles aim to establish a welfare state and promote social and economic justice. Articles included:

items:
• Article 38 – Promote welfare of the people
  • Article 39 – Adequate livelihood, equal pay, protection of children
  • Article 39A – Free legal aid
  • Article 41 – Right to work, education and public assistance
  • Article 42 – Just and humane conditions of work
  • Article 43 – Living wage for workers
  • Article 43A – Participation of workers in management

blocks.content: These principles aim to reduce inequalities and promote social justice.
GANDHIAN PRINCIPLES
These principles reflect the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and promote rural development. Articles included:

items:
• Article 40 – Organisation of Panchayats
  • Article 43 – Promotion of cottage industries
  • Article 46 – Protection of SCs, STs and weaker sections
  • Article 47 – Improvement of nutrition, public health
  • Article 48 – Prohibition of slaughter of cows

DPSP AND FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS
Initially, Fundamental Rights were given more importance than DPSPs. However, after various Supreme Court judgments:

items:
• Both FRs and DPSPs are considered complementary
  • DPSPs help in interpreting Fundamental Rights
  • Balance between individual rights and social welfare is maintained

blocks.content: IMPORTANT SUPREME COURT JUDGMENTS

items:
• Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951) – FRs are superior to DPSPs
  • Golaknath Case (1967) – Parliament cannot amend FRs
  • Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973) – Balance between FRs and DPSPs
  • Minerva Mills Case (1980) – Harmony between FRs and DPSPs is part of Basic Structure

blocks.content: IMPLEMENTATION OF DPSP
Many DPSPs have been implemented through laws such as:

items: Article 40 (Organisation of Panchayats), Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code), Article 45 (Early childhood education), and Article 50 (Separation of judiciary from executive) are frequently asked in exams.
Minerva Mills Case (1980) established that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs is a Basic Structure feature.
DPSPs are non-justiciable in nature, whereas Fundamental Rights are justiciable.

blocks.content: CONCLUSION

The Directive Principles of State Policy form the soul of the Indian Constitution. Though not enforceable by courts, they guide the State in establishing a just, socialistic and welfare- oriented society. Together with Fundamental Rights, DPSPs help achieve the goals of the Constitution.
